steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing Error Norm Truncation, a training objective that makes text generation models more robust to noisy training data. Motivate the problem with MLE, review how earlier work estimates data quality and where it falls short, introduce our method, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Text generation models and the MLE training paradigm
- Limitation of MLE: not robust to noisy training data
- Prior work: alternatives to MLE / modified MLE objectives using target-token probability
- Problem: ignoring the distribution of non-target tokens
- Our method: Error Norm Truncation (ENT)
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Text generation
  - success in downstream tasks: machine translation (cite), summarization (cite), question answering (cite), story generation (cite)
  - training paradigm: maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE), maximize probability of each training token given context
- MLE limitation
  - forced to put non-zero probability on all training tokens regardless of quality -> not robust to errors
  - vulnerable to natural noise: misspelled, misordered words (cite)
  - and adversarial noise: poisoned training data (cite)
- Prior work
  - alternatives to autoregressive MLE (cite) or modified MLE objective (cite)
  - modifications use predicted probability of ground truth token as data quality: high prob -> likely clean
  - remove high-loss data (cite) or down-weigh low-probability data (cite) each iteration
- Problem with that
  - ignores distribution of non-target tokens
  - low probability can mean high-entropy context with many continuations -> diluted (Figure 1, first example)
  - or model not converged yet (Figure 1, second example)
  - truncating / down-weighing then harmful
- ENT
  - \ell_{2} norm of difference between predicted distribution and one-hot ground truth -> data quality each iteration, truncate low quality
  - truncate tokens with low probability where model is confident it should be another token (Figure 1, third example)
  - token-level quality estimate, removes noisy tokens
- Contributions (three)
  - ENT: truncation guided by quality estimate that uses non-target distribution
  - consistently beats MLE and strong baselines across tasks and setups
  - MT robustness against two noise types: untranslated and randomly shuffled targets; beats previous truncation methods

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Neural text generation models have made a lot of progress and have had remarkable success in many downstream tasks, including but not limited to machine translation, summarization, question answering and story generation. The usual way to train text generation models is maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE), which finds the parameters that maximize the probability of each token in the training data given a context.

The problem with MLE is that the model has to assign a non-zero probability to all the tokens that appear in the training data, no matter what their quality is, and so the model is not robust to errors in the training data. Research has shown that text generation models are vulnerable to natural noise, for example misspelled and misordered words, and also to adversarial noise, for example poisoned training data.

To get around this limitation, previous studies have either looked for alternatives to the autoregressive MLE paradigm or they modify the MLE objective. The modifications of MLE estimate the quality of the data using the predicted probabilities of the ground truth token during training, where a high probability means a higher likelihood that the ground truth token is clean, and the other way around. So we can either just remove data with high loss, or down-weigh data with low probability at each training iteration, to make the model more robust to data noise.

- Problem: target-token probability ignores non-target distribution
  - low prob may be high-entropy context, many continuations, diluted (Figure 1 first example)
  - or model not converged (Figure 1 second example)
  - truncating / down-weighing harmful in both
- ENT
  - \ell_{2} norm of (predicted distribution - one-hot ground truth) as quality, truncate low quality each iteration
  - low prob + confident it should be another token (Figure 1 third example)
  - token-level, removes noisy tokens
- Contributions (threefold)
  - ENT method
  - beats MLE and strong baselines across tasks/setups
  - MT robustness to untranslated and randomly shuffled targets, beats previous truncation methods

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Neural text generation models have made a lot of progress and have had remarkable success in many downstream tasks, including but not limited to machine translation, summarization, question answering and story generation. The usual way to train text generation models is maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE), which finds the parameters that maximize the probability of each token in the training data given a context.

The problem with MLE is that the model has to assign a non-zero probability to all the tokens that appear in the training data, no matter what their quality is, and so the model is not robust to errors in the training data. Research has shown that text generation models are vulnerable to natural noise, for example misspelled and misordered words, and also to adversarial noise, for example poisoned training data.

To get around this limitation, previous studies have either looked for alternatives to the autoregressive MLE paradigm or they modify the MLE objective. The modifications of MLE estimate the quality of the data using the predicted probabilities of the ground truth token during training, where a high probability means a higher likelihood that the ground truth token is clean, and the other way around. So we can either just remove data with high loss, or down-weigh data with low probability at each training iteration, to make the model more robust to data noise.

But if we estimate data quality only with the predicted probability of the target token, we ignore the distribution of the non-target tokens. For example, when the model gives a low probability to some token, it could be that the context is high-entropy and has many possible continuations, which dilutes the probability of the target token (the first example in Figure 1). Another possibility is that the model has not converged enough yet and so it has not learned a reasonable distribution for this token (the second example in Figure 1). In both of these cases, truncating the token or down-weighing its loss could hurt model training.

So that the predicted distribution of non-target tokens is also considered when estimating data quality, we propose Error Norm Truncation (ENT). This modified objective uses the \ell_{2} norm of the difference between the predicted distribution of the model and the one-hot vector of the ground truth to measure data quality at each training iteration, and it truncates the data with low quality. Intuitively, our method truncates the tokens where the model gives a low probability but is also very confident that it should be some other token (the third example in Figure 1). ENT makes training more robust to data noise because it estimates data quality accurately at the token level and removes noisy tokens.

Our contributions are the following three:

- We propose Error Norm Truncation, a method that truncates data during training, guided by a more accurate data quality estimation that considers the probability distribution of non-target tokens;

- With experiments on different tasks and setups, we show that Error Norm Truncation consistently does better than the MLE baseline and also strong baselines from previous methods in generation quality;

- We directly validate that Error Norm Truncation makes machine translation models more robust against two different types of noise, untranslated and randomly shuffled target sentences, and it does better than all previous methods that truncate data.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Advances in neural text generation models have achieved remarkable success in many downstream tasks, including but not limited to machine translation [1], summarization [2], question answering [3] and story generation [4]. The prevalent paradigm for training text generation models is maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE), which finds the parameters that maximize the probability of each token from the training data conditioned on a given context.

The limitation of MLE is that the model is forced to assign a non-zero probability to all tokens that appear in the training data, regardless of their quality, which makes the model not robust to errors in the training data. Existing research has shown that text generation models are vulnerable to natural noise, such as misspelled and misordered words [5], and to adversarial noise, such as poisoned training data [6,7,8].

To overcome this limitation, previous studies have either explored alternatives to the autoregressive MLE paradigm [9,10,11] or modified the MLE objective [12,13,14,15,16,17,18]. Modifications of MLE estimate data quality using the predicted probabilities of the ground truth token during training: a high probability corresponds to a higher likelihood that the ground truth token is clean, and vice versa. We can therefore either directly remove data with high loss [14,19,20] or down-weigh data with low probability [21,18] at each training iteration to improve robustness to data noise.

However, estimating data quality using only the predicted probability of the target token ignores the distribution of the non-target tokens. For example, when a model assigns a low probability to a specific token, the context may be high-entropy with many viable continuations, which dilutes the probability of the target token (first example in Figure 1). Alternatively, the model may not have sufficiently converged and thus has not learned a reasonable distribution for this token (second example in Figure 1). In both cases, truncating this token or down-weighing its loss could be harmful to model training.

To take the predicted distribution of non-target tokens into account when estimating data quality, we propose Error Norm Truncation (ENT). This modified objective uses the \ell_{2} norm of the difference between the model's predicted distribution and the one-hot vector of the ground truth to measure data quality at each training iteration, and truncates data with low quality. Intuitively, our method truncates tokens to which the model not only assigns a low probability but is also very confident should be another token (third example in Figure 1). ENT improves robustness to data noise during training by accurately estimating data quality at the token level and removing noisy tokens.

In summary, our contribution is threefold:

- We propose Error Norm Truncation, a data truncation method during training guided by a more accurate data quality estimation method that considers the probability distribution of non-target tokens;

- Through experiments under different tasks and setups, we show that Error Norm Truncation consistently outperforms the MLE baseline as well as strong baselines proposed by previous methods in generation quality;

- We directly validate that Error Norm Truncation improves the robustness of machine translation models against two different types of noise, untranslated and randomly shuffled target sentences, and outperforms all previous methods that truncate data.
